conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:**
Yes, heavy current and former smokers are significantly less likely to die of lung cancer if they undergo regular screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). 

Large clinical trials and systematic evidence reviews consistently demonstrate that regular LDCT screening detects lung cancer at earlier, more treatable stages, leading to a substantial decrease in lung cancer mortality among high-risk individuals.

**Key Research Findings:**
* **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST):** A major randomized trial demonstrated that screening with low-dose CT reduced the risk of dying from lung cancer by 20% among long-time heavy smokers compared to screening with standard chest X-rays (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMcp1404071).
* **NELSON Trial:** The Dutch–Belgian randomized controlled trial confirmed that volume-based low-dose CT screening significantly reduces lung cancer mortality in high-risk heavy smokers (https://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item:3453624/view).
* **Systematic Reviews and Guidelines:** Meta-analyses of randomized trials show statistically significant evidence that low-dose CT screening reduces lung cancer mortality in adults with a smoking history of 20 or more pack-years (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11718421/).

**Sources:**
* *New England Journal of Medicine:* https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMcp1404071
* *NELSON Trial Report:* https://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item:3453624/view
* *Systematic Review on LDCT:* https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11718421/
